item.title: Collaboration Signatures: Tracking Long-Horizon Dynamics of Cross-Meeting Collaboration Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.10341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise platforms have received increasing attention as a core component of social networks and the Web. However, existing work mostly relies on fragmented logs of small units of work, like emails and chats, and focuses on who connects with whom without sufficient account of collaboration content and dynamics. This work systematically explores tracking collaborations across sequences of meetings as a new approach to interpreting their long-horizon dynamics. Linking 45,426 meetings in a large multinational technology company based on full transcripts and 1.6 million extracted agenda items, we establish a cross-meeting collaboration network of 6,065 collaborations. The network recovers the natural shapes of workplace collaborations: meetings, as snapshots of ongoing collaboration, link into largely tree-shaped structures, while the work content forms nested directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Further, we explore how these networks evolve over time, examining three established perspectives: task division, team composition, and temporal continuity. Each explains part of the dynamics but does not capture the distinctness of long-horizon workplace collaboration: e.g., work flows in a consistent direction between a few pairs of subjects, yet a collaboration's subject explains little of how its meetings are conducted. Instead, accumulating the agenda, interaction, and language of meetings along each tree yields a signature of the collaboration, a distinctive profile that picks out the collaboration of a held-out meeting at 4.5 times chance. The signature models collaboration better than team or task views, individually or combined, in next-meeting prediction and tree-level fitting. We discuss the implications of these cross-meeting dynamics for designing office applications and support tools, and call for next-generation Web systems that represent collaborations over their long horizon.
item.dc:creator: Shengqi Zhu, Sheshera Mysore, Bahareh Sarrafzadeh

item.title: Can open citation data detect citation stacking? An audit against Clarivate's journal suppressions
item.description: arXiv:2611.10471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clarivate suppresses journals from the Journal Citation Reports when self-citations or concentrated citations from another journal ("citation stacking") distort their Journal Impact Factor. Its data are closed. Yearly journal citation networks were built from the OpenCitations snapshot of January 2024 (1.96 billion citations; 85,437 journals) and compared with Clarivate's suppression lists for data years 2015-2023, collected from primary sources. Where reference lists are present, open data reproduce Clarivate's published self-citation shares within ten points for 36 of 50 journals. The failures follow publishers that do not deposit references with Crossref, which also hides several stacking donors. Biodiversity data downloads registered with DataCite inflate naive impact-factor numerators of taxonomy journals. The leading open method, CIDRE, detects none of 15 named Clarivate pairs: it drops large donor journals, and lowering its donor threshold merges the pairs into large groups. A recipient-centric reading of CIDRE's own test flags stacking-listed journals 6 to 14 times more often than other journals, depending on consensus level, and 5 to 7 times more often than size-matched controls, sometimes years before the listing. At equal flag rate it finds more listed journals than a plain 43% donor-share rule (10 vs 3 of 28), and about as many as a rule with a citation floor. A prospective check on the 2024-2025 lists agrees in direction but is not significant (one of six). Flagged pairs show more citations per citing paper and weaker topical similarity than matched pairs. Open audits are feasible if coverage gaps are reported.
item.dc:creator: Hossein Mohasel Arjomandi

item.title: Do links to retracted papers predict future retractions? An out-of-sample test on the open biomedical citation graph
item.description: arXiv:2611.10474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tools that screen manuscripts for research-integrity problems flag papers that cite retracted work, and retrospective studies report that such papers are retracted more often. This study tests the signal prospectively on open data. Predictors were computed on the January 2024 OpenCitations graph using the retractions known at that date, frozen, and compared with retractions in the Retraction Watch database from February 2024 to October 2026. The design was pre-specified. Among 10.5 million biomedical papers published 2015-2023, 2.1% cited a paper already retracted, and 4,323 were retracted later (0.041%). Citing a retracted paper raised the later retraction rate from 0.035% to 0.27% with one such reference; excluding reviews (post hoc), it rose to 2.3% with five or more. Within journal and publication year the odds ratio was 2.99 (95% CI 2.73-3.27), and 3.03 when reference-list length was also held fixed (post hoc), so the signal is not explained by retraction waves in journals or by long reference lists. As a screen it is weak: 0.9% of the 1,000 highest-ranked papers were retracted later (2.2% with reviews set aside, post hoc), and 84% of later retractions cite no retracted paper. When the time point was moved into the late-2023 retraction wave, the journal's own retraction rate became the far better screen. NIH-funded papers cited already-retracted work as often as other papers in the same journal and year. Links to retracted papers are a useful flag but not a screen on their own.
item.dc:creator: Hossein Mohasel Arjomandi

item.title: Place and Political Behavior Online during the Los Angeles Blaze
item.description: arXiv:2611.10631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how online communication during extreme weather crises enables or constrains climate mobilization is critical. During a crisis, the online world connects distant audiences and complicates the relationship between place and political behavior. We analyze all sociopolitical content from Bluesky about the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfire event, reporting how participation in collective action and allocation of attention vary by geographic distance. Participation varies nonlinearly with proximity, with local and international users participating more than regional and national users. Attention concentrates around regional and national users engaging primarily in viral, non-participatory political discussion. Analysis reveals a geographic mismatch between participation and attention, illuminating how online communication concentrates attention away from collective action amid an exacerbating climate crisis.
item.dc:creator: Sofi Koponen, Ali Salloum, Luca Maria Aiello, Mikko Kivel\"a, Arttu Malkam\"aki

item.title: Who Benefits from Wikipedia's Growth Mentorship? The Role of Newcomer Information Needs
item.description: arXiv:2611.11083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of Wikipedia's programs for new editors usually ask whether a program works on average; we ask which newcomers benefit when their question to a mentor gets a reply. English Wikipedia's Growth mentorship system assigns every new account a volunteer mentor, and about a quarter of the questions newcomers send never get a reply. Using the first questions of 34,073 newcomers (2021 to 2026), we compare newcomers who received a reply with similar newcomers who did not, matched on 164 characteristics recorded before the question (propensity score stratification). (1) Does a reply help newcomers keep editing? Yes, in the short term: in the 14 days after the reply, newcomers who received one were 1.8 percentage points (pp) more likely to edit an article (22% vs. an estimated 20% without a reply) and 1.8pp more likely to edit on two or more days. Later in the first year, the only difference that remains significant after correction for multiple testing is in the share who edit an article at least once between six months and one year after the reply (+1.5pp). (2) Does the effect depend on what the newcomer asked? Yes. We sort questions by Morrison's (1993) information-seeking types, which earlier studies measured mostly through self-reports, using a language model checked against human labels. A reply has significant effects for questions about rules and norms (+3.4pp), questions that show the newcomer's earlier editing (+3.4pp) and specific how-to questions (+2.4pp). For newcomers who do not know what to work on, a reply has no detectable effect, and the effect is 4.2pp smaller than for newcomers with other questions. (3) Which replies are followed by more editing? Among newcomers who received a reply, those whose reply came sooner or stayed closer to the topic of their question edited more.
item.dc:creator: Yubo Zhou, Pengyu Chen, Ceren Budak

item.title: The AI research space shapes country academic performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.11663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have demonstrated great potential across diverse domains, prompting increasing attention to understanding the AI ecosystem. As knowledge production is often perceived as a process of connecting existing pieces of knowledge, mapping the interconnections of AI knowledge is crucial for unraveling the dynamics of scientific production in AI. However, maps created so far have fallen short of capturing knowledge relatedness, focusing instead on citation relationships between subfields. Here, we build an AI research space by connecting pairs of AI research topics based on their proximity measured through author-topic coupling. Projections of country level performances onto the space reveal that countries exhibit distinct baskets of specializations. We further examine the role of the structure of the AI research space in the scientific development of nations. We find that countries are more likely to gain specialization in topics that have high proximity to already specialized neighbor topics, and that publications whose topics align more with the developed topics in the country are more likely to become high impact. Our results highlight the AI development gaps across nations and the path-dependence in the development induced by the AI research space.
item.dc:creator: Siyi Zhou, Tianxing Pan, Qing Ke

item.title: The Radicalization Pipeline: Characterizing and Predicting Online Misogyny
item.description: arXiv:2611.12797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social media platforms are known to shape and polarize user opinions and, increasingly, facilitate pathways toward ideological extremism. Among these trends, online misogynistic communities associ- ated with the incel (involuntary celibate) ideology have received growing scholarly attention. Previous work has primarily focused on ideological narratives and linguistic content within incel communities them- selves. However, much less is known about how user behaviors evolve over time, particularly before and after their engagement with incel spaces, and whether early signals can anticipate such transitions. In this study, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of Reddit users who participated in the r/incels community on Reddit. Our results show that engagement with the incel community is associated with a substantial in- crease in toxicity in both posts and comments, while hate increases particularly in posts after engagement. These changes extend beyond explicitly ideological communities: users who engage with the r/incels sub- reddit display elevated toxicity and hate speech even in subreddits related to leisure, entertainment, and everyday interests. In parallel, user activity shifts away from recreational and support-oriented communi- ties toward subreddits focused on social issues, indicating a broader reorientation of online participation. Finally, we show that future incel users can be identified with high accuracy prior to engagement using supervised machine learning models trained on linguistic, contextual, and interaction-based features. These findings suggest that online misogynistic radicalization follows detectable behavioral trajectories and diffuses across the broader social media ecosystem.
item.dc:creator: Anna Bertani, Nathan Ratkiewicz, Alessandro Flammini, Filippo Menczer

item.title: GSynPEF: A Privacy Evaluation Framework for Synthetic Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.10185v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: It is often desirable to generate and release synthetic graphs, which resemble real-world data, in a privacy-preserving way. While substantial progress has been made in designing private graph synthesizers (PGS), opportunities remain for more explicit connections between synthesizer models and privacy evaluation, and better accounting for output variation. This paper proposes GSynPEF, a practical framework for empirical evaluation of privacy and utility in settings for which a real-world graph is given as input and output synthetic graph(s) are observed. Our framework links a broad class of graph synthesizers (both statistical and deep-learning based) with privacy metrics, expanding evaluation dimensions to practical utility and risk, through empirical analysis of multiple actual outputs. The framework accommodates both an Exact Solution scenario, where synthesizer behavior is directly observable, and a Monte Carlo Approximation scenario where only synthetic outputs from a black box synthesizer are available. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets and seven widely used graph synthesizers demonstrate framework's versatility, enabling privacy evaluation for different attack goals (e.g., to infer an edge or node) and capabilities (e.g., observing one or multiple synthetic graphs). We analyze evaluation results by examining the relationship between graph statistics and synthesizer design choices, providing insights for data curators in PGS selection and researchers for improved PGS design.
item.dc:creator: Yu Duan, Luca Baldesi, Carter T. Butts, Athina Markopoulou

item.title: Police Behavior Patterns Through Radio Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.10322v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the United States, most police departments communicate using police radio, which allows for officer-to-officer and officer-to-dispatch communication without depending on cellular network or WiFi availability. While some departments use encrypted digital radio, many continue to transmit in the clear, and are legally monitored by public citizens with `police scanners.' Because police radio is intended for internal police use and represents real-time communication, it may offer valuable insight into patterns of law enforcement activities without the potential bias and filtering introduced by a press release after the fact. In this study, we collect and examine over 14 million radio transmissions representing over 100,000 hours of speech by officers in 34 cities across the United States from July 2025 through July 2026; to our knowledge the largest scale analysis of Broadcast Police Communication (BPC) to date. We highlight both typical patterns of police communication and categorize anomalous activity that represents incidents including protests and major weather events. We present this dataset as a starting point for an array of police communication studies, conduct our own preliminary analysis, and propose several further areas of inquiry.
item.dc:creator: Milo Z. Trujillo, Adam Perhala, Elaine Zou, Tyler Mckenzie, Juniper Lovato, Brooke Foucault Welles, Alyssa Hasegawa Smith

item.title: Regularity in Cryptocurrency Market Cycles: A Halving-to-Halving Analysis Using Data from Google Trends and Wikipedia
item.description: arXiv:2611.10674v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bitcoin halvings provide a natural temporal structure for studying long-term dynamics of cryptocurrency markets. This paper presents a methodological framework for analyzing the regularity of Bitcoin and aggregate cryptocurrency market cycles by normalizing historical periods between consecutive halving events and projecting them onto a common relative-time scale expressed as the percentage of cycle completion. The proposed framework integrates market variables, namely Bitcoin price and aggregate cryptocurrency market capitalization, with measures of public attention derived from Google Trends search volume and Wikipedia pageviews. To obtain long-horizon daily attention indices, Google Trends data are reconstructed from overlapping 90-day windows linked by median scale ratios, following established approaches to combining high-frequency Google Trends samples. Rather than attempting to forecast future prices, the study aims to compare historical cycles, identify recurring temporal patterns, and evaluate the relationship between market dynamics and retail investor interest across different cycle-relative stages. Exploratory results point to a possible recurring structure. The maxima of the aggregate market capitalization in the two most recent completed cycles occurred at 39.0% and 37.9% of cycle completion, and the highest value of the ongoing cycle observed to date at 38.1% (534-547 days after the respective halvings), although the corresponding multiple of the halving-day value fell from 66 to 1.8. Public attention shows a similar compression of peak multiples, but not a similar timing. The paper also discusses current data limitations and outlines future research directions, including formal lead-lag analyses and expanded multi-asset investigations.
item.dc:creator: Marek Zatwarnicki, Piotr Stolarski, W{\l}odzimierz Lewoniewski

item.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
item.description: arXiv:2611.10808v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Drishti Goel, Ethan M. Nguyen, Violeta J. Rodriguez, Koustuv Saha

item.title: Evolutionary games on networks with negative edge-based environmental feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.11029v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Environmental feedback can fundamentally alter the game payoff structure underlying the evolution of cooperation. How feedback-evolving games interact with population structure under non-weak selection remains incompletely understood. We study an evolutionary game on networks in which each edge has a binary environmental state that determines the payoff matrix used by the two connected individuals. By assumption, cooperation tends to improve the local environment, which in turn favors defection, thereby creating negative feedback between strategies coupled with the environmental condition. We analyze the model under strong selection using a mean-field approximation, a pair approximation that tracks both strategy pairs and edge environments, and agent-based simulations. In well-mixed populations, the feedback can generate bistability between full cooperation and full defection, as well as sustained oscillations arising through a Hopf bifurcation. Sparse networks (i.e., with low nodes' degrees) can eliminate bistability, suppress oscillations, and produce stable intermediate levels of cooperation. The pair approximation captures these effects and generally agrees more closely with simulations on sparse networks than the mean-field approximation. Our results show that edge-based environmental feedback and network structure, such as density of edges, interact to determine whether the fraction of cooperators stabilizes or oscillates over time.
item.dc:creator: Katherine Betz, Feng Fu, Naoki Masuda

item.title: Retrospective Analysis of Team-Following Trading Profitability in Pumpfun Meme Coins Using Funding Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11436v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: If the right token-creation teams had been known, how much could following them have returned, and what is left when only information available before each launch is used? We study ten separately recorded Pumpfun windows (April 2024 to September 2026), each reconstructed independently from real-SOL reserve states and finite-capital accounts that start with one SOL. Teams are directed funding groups ranked in hindsight. When every team exits at its own best reserve threshold, chosen in hindsight, the main account ends above one SOL in all 8 windows that have a qualifying team (1.10 to 11.32 SOL), but free cash exceeds one SOL in only 5, and marks of positions that never reached their threshold make up 17--94% of equity. If teams are recognised online, from tokens whose first hour has completed, 9 of 19 teams become identifiable only after their last launch; the remaining 10 end above one SOL in 10 cases, with free cash above one SOL in 7; funding links in this step still come from the full window, so even these results are not a fully realisable signal. A large model balance, a result above random cohorts that repeat the threshold search, and a statistical rejection in the selection-matched nulls (3 of 40 tests after Holm adjustment) are three different statements, and these nulls condition on the discovered funding graph, so they do not calibrate the whole selection procedure. Midpoint tests describe a further source of apparent opportunity. A detailed analysis of the best and the worst window, with every analysis parameter varied, shows that the worst result, which is close to break-even, rises several-fold with a stop rule or another funding-graph construction. The results are conditional retrospective model accounts, not executable profits, and not evidence of a causal effect of the SOL price.
item.dc:creator: Fail Gafarov

item.title: Continuous modeling of manipulative participation for stance analysis: Online discourse on the 2024 Street Animal Law in T\"urkiye
item.description: arXiv:2611.11576v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Studies of online political discourse commonly infer public opinion through stance analysis while implicitly assuming that observed user participation is authentic. Meanwhile, studies focusing on detecting manipulative participation are typically modeling it as a binary phenomenon, overlooking the varying degrees to which users may engage in coordinated or inauthentic behavior. This study proposes a continuous modeling approach for manipulative participation and examines its integration with stance analysis. Using online discourse on the 2024 Street Animal Law in T\"urkiye as a case study, we collected a dataset comprising 7,320,574 tweets from 537,994 users. From this corpus, 301 users were selected through a high-information sampling strategy and manually annotated by domain experts using a 10-criterion rubric that yields user-level continuous manipulative participation scores. Evaluation under a unified user-level cross-validation protocol showed that the proposed framework accurately estimates both manipulative participation and user stance, with gradient boosting methods providing the best manipulative participation estimates and BERTurk achieving the highest stance classification performance. External validation on an independently annotated user set demonstrated good generalization performance. The findings support modeling manipulative participation as a continuous construct rather than a binary label, providing a more informative basis for computational analyses of the relationship between manipulative participation and stance in online political discourse.
item.dc:creator: Ulya Bayram, Ebru Belk{\i}s G\"uzelo\u{g}lu, Emel Ku\c{s}ku \"Ozdemir, Elif \"Ust\"unda\u{g}l{\i} Erten, \"Oyk\"um Esra Yi\u{g}it

item.title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.11714v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.
item.dc:creator: Sepehr Ilami, Babak Heydari

item.title: Computational Structure of Pairwise Housing Connectedness Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.12189v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Directed housing-submarket networks combine common market movement with heterogeneous bilateral relations, and different node-level measures need not yield distinct empirical rankings. We construct a positive pairwise net-connectedness network from the generalized forecast error variance decomposition (GFEVD) of a vector autoregression (VAR) and use it to compare complementary node positions. Net directional connectedness (NET), PageRank, and Viral Centrality summarize net directional balance, recursively weighted incoming position, and normalized multistep reach. When bilateral net differences are nonzero, the network is a weighted tournament. A least-squares edge-flow decomposition separates the pairwise-net matrix into a NET-equivalent gradient component and a NET-orthogonal residual, while a monotone-allocation condition establishes exact PageRank-indegree correspondence in a transitive tournament. In Seoul's 25-district network, the gradient component accounts for 70.9% of the squared Frobenius norm, leaving 29.1% in the residual component. PageRank is strongly aligned with indegree (Spearman $\rho=0.987$), and Viral Centrality with outdegree ($\rho=0.935$); the PageRank alignment exceeds the range of independently weighted simulations with comparable tournament consistency and edge-weight variation. Three common-component treatments reduce total connectedness from 81.98% to 50.60-52.00%, a 36.6-38.3% reduction relative to the raw system, and reverse 97-98 of 300 pairwise net directions. Thus, both the magnitude and the apparent direction of connectedness depend materially on the treatment of citywide common movement. Songpa's positive NET position remains prominent across common-component treatments and dynamic specifications and ranks first in both chronological subsamples.
item.dc:creator: Seo In Jang, Seung Ho Choi, Ji-Eun Shin, Hyunwoo Lee

item.title: Resetting-based designated information distribution
item.description: arXiv:2611.12485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a network of $n$ nodes under random gossip dynamics, we show that by introducing the additional resetting mechanism (with rate $\beta$) to a designated subset of $r$ nodes, the expected sum of all node values is asymptotically equal to $\tfrac{n}{r}$ times the sum of the initial values of the $r$ designated nodes, in the small-$\beta$ and long-time limit. We also analyze the convergence speed to this asymptotic state and provide an approximate high-probability confidence interval for the expected sum at finite time $t$ and finite $\beta$. Operationally, we propose a protocol that distributes the initial node values over the designated subset evenly (up to a prescribed precision), by appropriately turning on and off the resetting dynamics. Our work not only offers insights into classical problems such as distributed computing and network control, but also serves as a potential foundation for designing quantum algorithms that prepare desired states in quantum networks using only local operations.
item.dc:creator: Xiaojuan Ma, Yan Wang, Indranil Gupta

item.title: SnapScope: A Platform for City-Scale Collection and Exploration of Public Snap Map Data
item.description: arXiv:2608.05841v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Snapchat's Snap Map is an ephemeral stream of geotagged public video and image stories. The platform documents no API for it, no prior work describes a reproducible way to collect it at city scale, and no tool exists for exploring what is collected. We present SnapScope, which pairs a collection back end with a web front end. The back end builds a geographic query grid, sweeps it on a schedule, and deduplicates at ingestion; the front end supports scraper management, interactive exploration, neighborhood comparison, and export. Deployed over Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, it collected 515,364 unique public snaps across 23 days (17 September-9 October 2024) on a 1 km grid of 2,740 query points. A saturation probe over 21 consecutive runs found 94.8% of returned observations already stored, indicating that successive passes mostly return already-captured content. We release a privacy-safe aggregate dataset of tile-level hourly counts under CC BY 4.0. The platform is city-agnostic: redeployment requires only new grid coordinates and boundary polygons.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Almukaynizi, Fahad Alhaqbani, Khaled Almarzoug, Sultan Alanbari

item.title: Counting Hypertriangles through Hypergraph Orientations
item.description: arXiv:2601.03573v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Counting the number of small patterns is a central task in network analysis. While this problem is well studied for graphs, many real-world datasets are naturally modeled as hypergraphs, motivating the need for efficient hypergraph motif counting algorithms. In particular, we study the problem of counting hypertriangles - collections of three pairwise-intersecting hyperedges. These hypergraph patterns have a rich structure with multiple distinct intersection patterns unlike graph triangles. Inspired by classical graph algorithms based on orientations and degeneracy, we develop a new theoretical framework that generalizes these concepts to hypergraphs and yields provable algorithms for hypertriangle counting. We implement these ideas in DITCH (Degeneracy Inspired Triangle Counter for Hypergraphs) and show experimentally that it is faster on all but one small instance, achieving speedups of up to 100x, and is 6-100x more memory-efficient than existing state-of-the-art methods.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Paul-Pena, Vaishali Surianarayanan, Deeparnab Chakrabarty, C. Seshadhri

item.title: Spectral Graph Sparsification Preserves Representation Geometry in Graph Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2605.01136v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spectral graph sparsification is a classical tool for reducing graph complexity while preserving Laplacian quadratic forms. In graph neural networks (GNNs), sparsification is often used to accelerate computation while maintaining predictive performance. In this work, we study a complementary representation-level question: does sparsification preserve the geometry of learned embeddings? For polynomial-filter GNNs, we prove that any $\epsilon$-spectral sparsifier induces $O(\epsilon)$ perturbations in polynomial graph filters, multilayer hidden representations, and their Gram matrices. These guarantees imply stability of squared pairwise distances, class means, and covariance structure in embedding space. We further establish finite-time training stability: under smoothness and boundedness assumptions, gradient descent on dense and sparsified graphs produces weight trajectories whose separation grows at most proportionally to the sparsification distortion. Empirically, effective-resistance sparsification validates the predicted perturbation chain on synthetic graphs and preserves hidden representation geometry on real datasets. In our experiments, the gram matrix and training dynamics show low divergence even under substantial sparsification, consistent with the predicted stability under spectral sparsification. Hidden Gram preservation strongly predicts neighborhood preservation and class-centroid stability across FashionMNIST, Cora, and Paul15. Together, these results show that spectral sparsification preserves not only graph operators, but also the representation geometry that supports downstream use of GNN embeddings for interpretability.
item.dc:creator: Sanjukta Krishnagopal

item.title: Modelling Opinion Dynamics at Scale with Deep MARL
item.description: arXiv:2606.07487v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modelling opinion dynamics typically relies on hand-crafted local interaction rules to study emergent macroscopic phenomena such as consensus and polarisation. In contrast, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables agents to learn such behaviours directly by optimising simple rewards. To explore the potential of MARL for opinion dynamics, we introduce a GPU-accelerated consensus and truth-finding game that scales to populations of up to 1000 agents, comparable to many real-world social sub-networks. To prevent unrealistic conventions, we extend other-play to general-sum social interactions. We next validate our model on a subset of the Bluesky network by recovering agent importance structures from graph topology alone via a learned attention layer, finding that highly conforming populations most closely match human data. In large social media networks, such high levels of conformity significantly reduce collective accuracy and promote dishonest agents that lie to fit in. By contrast, small hunter-gatherer networks are less affected; here, conformity can even improve collective agreement. This suggests a mismatch between evolved human conformity heuristics and modern social media environments as a potential contributor to misinformation.
item.dc:creator: Lukas Seier, Brandon Kaplowitz, Sebastian Towers, Richard Bailey, Jakob Foerster

item.title: Governing Well in the Algorithmic Age: The Foundations of Digital Statecraft
item.description: arXiv:2607.18483v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The digital substrate - data, algorithms, infrastructure, platforms, applications - is being governed without adequate conceptual foundations. The ability and legitimacy required to govern this substrate, and to govern with it, are simultaneously misaligned, contested, and structurally absent. We introduce digital statecraft as the organising concept for this emerging field, arguing that 'digital' reconstitutes the statecraft question rather than merely extending its domain. The concept operates on two dimensions - statecraft over digital systems, concerning the authority and capacity of the state in relation to the digital substrate itself, and statecraft with digital systems, concerning the deployment of algorithmic tools as instruments of governing authority. And it rests on two foundational requirements, technical coherence and legitimate authority, that are genuinely in tension. We derive ten principles of digital statecraft from these foundations, each naming a condition whose absence produces an identifiable and structural governance failure: public interest first, human-machine complementarity, governability by design, systemic coherence, hybrid institutions, adaptive governance, human centricity and civic agency, accountable and traceable authority, judgment across time, and the non-delegable core. This article takes the state as the starting point, the institutional form that developed historically in response to the problem of effective and legitimate public governance, and the only current candidate for which the full set of legitimacy conditions is institutionally available. But the digital statecraft programme holds open a deeper question than just whether states can reform themselves: governing well in the algorithmic age may require rethinking the boundaries, scale, and affiliative basis of statehood itself.

item.title: Toward a Unified Statistical Theory of Multi-View Pretraining for Neural Knowledge Graph Learning
item.description: arXiv:2607.26346v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowledge graph learning offers a powerful framework for representing and inferring structured knowledge, with broad practical applications. Two obstacles limit current methods: labeled triples are scarce for each entity and relation, which makes expressive models hard to train, and scoring functions are designed ad hoc, which limits their generalizability and leaves them without theoretical grounding. We address both obstacles with a theoretically grounded framework, with end-to-end guarantees, that extends and subsumes existing methods. The framework proceeds in two stages: multi-view unsupervised pretraining that integrates heterogeneous sources of entity side information into a shared representation, followed by supervised learning across multiple relation types. We establish a unified nonasymptotic risk bound that combines the subspace recovery error of pretraining and the sample complexity of the labeled data in a single guarantee, quantifying formally how large-scale unlabeled data from multiple views benefits downstream knowledge prediction. Synthetic experiments validate each component of the theory, and experiments on large-scale real-world knowledge graph benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Jifan Zhang, Miklos Racz, Suqi Liu

item.title: ConnectionMind: Leveraging Social Networks and Large Language Models for Personalized Recommendation at Meta
item.description: arXiv:2608.10187v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern recommendation systems on social media platforms such as Meta must model complex social relationships, including friendships, group memberships, and creator interactions, alongside massive and heterogeneous content such as text and video. Traditional recommendation models, however, often omit these signals or treat them independently, lacking the reasoning capability to integrate multi-relational context for fine-grained personalization. We present ConnectionMind, a production-ready recommendation framework that tightly integrates the social network structure with large language models (LLMs) to enable scalable, interpretable, and reasoning-aware personalization in Meta. ConnectionMind constructs a heterogeneous graph connecting users, items, friends, groups, and creator pages, and formulates recommendation as a graph reasoning problem: discovering personalized paths from users to candidate items. An LLM-based policy is employed to reason over these graph structures and guide recommendation decisions. To train the system at scale, ConnectionMind adopts a two-stage learning strategy. We first perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on large-scale user-item interaction trajectories to initialize the reasoning policy, followed by end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) to refine the model's ability to reason over social graphs for personalized recommendation. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ConnectionMind compared to representative baselines. More importantly, ConnectionMind has been deployed in Meta's large-scale recommendation pipeline and has been evaluated through online A/B tests, achieving a 0.43% improvement in video watch time. These results demonstrate measurable real-world impact in a production recommendation system.
item.dc:creator: Haoyu Han, Yuming Liu, Lei Huang, Lizhu Zhang, Jiliang Tang, Xiangjun Fan

item.title: A learner-free swarm approximates the explore-exploit equilibrium allocation: A self-organized attractor in place of reinforcement-learning machinery
item.description: arXiv:2610.25113v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) solves the explore-exploit problem by training a learner on reward; its multi-agent, resource-sharing form has an equilibrium allocation as its optimum -- the ideal-free distribution (IFD), the Nash equilibrium of a congestion game. We show a minimal swarm approximates it with no learner at all. We present a decentralized, learner-free method for this problem: agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a degree-normalized threshold cascade, and disperse as a patch crowds. The method drives the collective to the shape of the equilibrium allocation (pooled spatial matching slope 1.14, R^2=0.61) with no training, no stored parameters, and no reward in its dynamics; it reaches this as a self-organized attractor and holds it, re-finding it when the resources move -- though it reaches the shape, not the exact equilibrium, and stays measurably exploitable (Nash-gap 1.46). Coupling recruitment to movement causes the allocation: removing it collapses the matching (slope 0.006). Against Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) learners (feedforward, centralized-critic, graph message-passing, and recurrent) trained in the same sensing-limited environment, the method at zero training is the only arm left unbiased w.r.t. the IFD gradient (slope ~1, CI containing 1, vs learners 0.69-0.97, all under-concentrating) and ties the best learner's harvest where resource is clustered, while the learner collects more where resource is scarce (0.33 vs 0.22) and holds a tighter per-capita intake. Learning buys precision and transfer across reward structures, not a better allocation shape. A companion paper develops the mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Galen J. Wilkerson
